name: Norse
intro: Norse myth reaches us mainly through two medieval Icelandic books: the Poetic Edda, a collection of older poems, and the Prose Edda, a handbook compiled by the scholar Snorri Sturluson. Both were written down in Christian Iceland in the thirteenth century, long after the pre-Christian religion had faded, so they preserve old material through a medieval lens. The stories describe nine worlds held together by the ash tree Yggdrasil: Asgard for the gods, Midgard for humans, Jotunheim for the giants, and others beneath and beyond. Their gods are not all-powerful. Odin gives an eye for wisdom and knows he will die at Ragnarök; Thor defends the worlds with his hammer; Loki both helps the gods and destroys them. Again and again these myths ask how people should act when the ending is already known. Their answer is courage, and luck.

timeline.label: Earliest traces
timeline.note: Runic inscriptions, coins, and helmet plates from Scandinavia and northern Europe hint at gods who would later be named Odin, Thor, and Freyr.

timeline.label: Viking Age
timeline.note: Norse religion is practised across Scandinavia and in every place Norse ships trade and raid; poems about gods and heroes circulate orally.

timeline.label: Christian conversion
timeline.note: Iceland and Norway formally adopt Christianity; traditional stories survive in poetry, law, and custom rather than in temple worship.

timeline.label: Prose Edda written
timeline.note: Snorri Sturluson writes Gylfaginning and Skáldskaparmál, retelling many myths and quoting older verse.

timeline.label: Poetic Edda compiled
timeline.note: An anonymous Icelandic manuscript, the Codex Regius, gathers older poems including Völuspá, Hávamál, and Þrymskviða.

timeline.label: Modern rediscovery
timeline.note: Manuscripts are collected and printed, and Norse myth becomes a major influence on European literature, art, and music.

sources.title: Poetic Edda, Völuspá
sources.note: The seeress's vision of creation and Ragnarök, and the main surviving poetic account of the world's end.

sources.title: Poetic Edda, Hávamál
sources.note: A collection of wisdom sayings that includes Odin's own account of hanging on the tree to win the runes.

sources.title: Poetic Edda, Þrymskviða
sources.note: The comic poem of Thor's stolen hammer, the bridal disguise, and the wedding feast in Jotunheim.

sources.title: Poetic Edda, Lokasenna
sources.note: Loki's insult contest with the gods at Ægir's hall, the scene that leads to his binding.

sources.title: Poetic Edda, Baldrs draumar
sources.note: Odin rides to the underworld and learns what the seeress knows about Baldr's coming death.

sources.title: Prose Edda, Gylfaginning
sources.note: Snorri Sturluson's systematic retelling of creation, the gods, Baldr's death, and Ragnarök.

sources.title: Prose Edda, Skáldskaparmál
sources.note: Snorri's guide to poetic language, which preserves many myths in the quotations it uses as examples.

sources.title: Codex Regius manuscript
sources.note: The thirteenth-century manuscript that preserves most of the Poetic Edda, copied in Christian Iceland.
